full_judgment:
3. Mr KS Nabi, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner has submitted that on the face of the allegations contained in the charge-sheet no misconduct had been committed by the petitioner and that the Labour Court acted without jurisdiction in upholding the order of dismissal. He has further submitted that the petitioner being not aware of the 'Production schedule' of Industrial Workers Wage Commission the order of dismissal ought not to have been maintained by the Labour Court. He has also submitted that the plea of the worker that low production, if any, resulted from the short supply of raw materials ought to have been accepted by the Labour Court. 

 We find that the charge-sheet clearly contained allegations that between 4-11-74 and 22-11-74 production given by petitioner had abnormally come down compared to the production given by the petitioner as per 'production schedule' set by Industrial workers wages commission. It was further alleged in the charge-sheet that the worker intentionally had been slowing down the production to half causing loss to the factory and to the prejudice production must have been laid in evidence in the enquiry made by the Enquiry Committee which we need not investigate here. We find from the order of dismissal that the management had cited therein the production figures of fours days to show that production has been slowed down and there has been a low production compared to IWWC production schedule. It is seen from the record that on receipt of written explanation submitted by the petitioner against the allegation, the Management held an impartial enquiry to enquire into the allegations. The petitioner appeared before the enquiry committee to defend himself. The enquiry committee found that there was no dearth of raw materials and that raw materials were regularly supplied to maintain the production schedule. The committee on consideration of materials on record found that the petitioner committed gross misconduct warranting dismissal. The finding of the Labour Court upholding the order of dismissal on the allegation that the petitioner adopted go slow tactics cannot be set-aside unless the enquiry was held unfairly and with prejudice to the petitioner. No allegation of an unfair enquiry has been made before this court. We, therefore, hold that the Labour Court rightly upheld the order of dismissal. 

 4. Mr Nabi has next submitted that prior permission form the Labour Court was required under section 18(7) of Bangladesh employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act 1965 to dismiss a worker for adopting go-slow tactics and that the employer having dismissed the worker without such prior permission in the present case, the order of dismissal was liable to be set-aside. 

 5. In our view provisions of section 18(7) of Bangladesh Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 gives an alternative power to the employer to dismiss collectively or individually any worker in case of misconduct of go-slow tactics or illegal strike without following the procedure of holding enquiry as laid down in section 18(1) of the Act. We also find the Labour Court has rightly found that the provision of section 18(7) does not in any way limit or effect the employer's right to take disciplinary action by himself after complying with the procedure of Section 18(1) of the said Act. The procedures prescribed in section 18(7) of the said Act are extraordinary and in addition to the procedures prescribed is section 18(1) of the said Act.
